newsitem.title: USA: Former Klansman executed in Alabama.
newsitem.headline: Former Klansman executed in Alabama.

text.p: Former Ku Klux Klansman Henry Francis Hays was executed on Friday, the first white man in Alabama to be put to death for murdering a black since 1913.
Hays, 42, told his brother he loved him and was strapped into the state electric chair at 1:10 a.m. EDT (0510 GMT), after refusing a last meal. He was pronounced dead eight minutes later.
He was killed for the 1981 lynching of Michael Donald, a murder that prosecutors said was intended to demonstrate Klan strength in the state.
His case also triggered a civil court judgment in which a Klan organisation was held liable for its members' actions and ordered to pay damages to a victim's family.
Hays claimed he was innocent and blamed his 1983 conviction on his membership in the United Klans of America.

But one of his fellow Klan members, James "Tiger" Knowles, testified at the murder trial that he and Hays cruised the poorer neighbourhoods of Mobile, Alabama, on March 20, 1981, looking for someone black to kill.

The victim they set upon was Donald, 19. The two men forced Donald into their car at gunpoint. They beat him with tree branches and, after he tried to escape, put a noose around his neck and choked him.
Knowles said Hays then slashed Donald's throat three times to make sure he was dead and tied his body up in a tree.
The jury of 11 whites and one black that convicted Hays also recommended a sentence of life without parole. But the trial judge overrode that recommendation and changed the penalty to death.
Knowles received a life sentence after pleading guilty to a federal charge of violating Donald's civil rights.
Hays' brother and sister this week made an unsuccessful appeal for clemency to Alabama Gov. Fob James, blaming the crime on their late father.

The father, Bennie Jack Hays, was leader of the United Klans in southern Alabama. He was charged with inciting Donald's murder. But a mistrial was declared in his case after he collapsed during the proceedings. He died before he could be tried again.
Another family member, Hays' brother-in-law Frank Cox, is serving a 99-year prison sentence for supplying the rope used in the slaying.

"I think the tragedy here was Bennie Hays, a man who orchestrated the whole thing. A very, very evil man ended up destroying his whole family," said Morris Dees, founder of the Southern Poverty Law Centre, which sued the United Klans over the Donald murder.
In the civil case, an all-white jury found United Klans responsible for the Donald murder. As a result, Donald's mother, Beulah Mae Donald, was awarded $7 million.
The damages effectively broke one of the largest Klan organisations and left the white supremacist group's Tuscaloosa, Alabama, headquarters building in the hands of the Donald family.
